monuments.name: Temple of Divus Claudius
monuments.builderName: begun by Agrippina; demolished by Nero; rebuilt by Vespasian

phases.t: converted into a nymphaeum by Nero

monuments.summary: Begun by Agrippina on the Caelian after Claudius' death and deification in 54, then largely demolished by Nero, who turned the east face of its huge terrace into a cascading nymphaeum for the Domus Aurea; Vespasian rebuilt it. The platform, about 200 by 180 m on arched substructures, still frames the Caelian: the church and monastery of Santi Giovanni e Paolo stand on its west side and the church's bell tower rises on its travertine arches. Seneca's Apocolocyntosis mocked the deification it served.

monuments.name: Temple of Quirinus
monuments.summary: Dedicated in 293 BC by the consul L. Papirius Cursor from Samnite spoils on the Quirinal; Pliny says Papirius set up Rome's first public sundial here. Caesar's statue was placed in it in 45 BC with the inscription 'to the unconquered god'. Burned in 49 BC, it was rebuilt by Augustus in 16 BC as a dipteral temple with 76 columns (Vitruvius 3.2.7).

monuments.name: Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
monuments.builderName: vowed by A. Postumius; dedicated by Sp. Cassius

phases.t: becomes the archive of senatus consulta

monuments.summary: Vowed by the dictator A. Postumius during the famine of 496 and dedicated in 493 BC by Sp. Cassius near the starting gates of the Circus Maximus. Decorated by the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus, it was the religious centre of the plebs: the plebeian aediles kept their offices and the archive of senatus consulta here (from 449 BC), fines from offenders against tribunes went to it, and it offered asylum. Burned in 31 BC, rebuilt by Augustus and dedicated by Tiberius in AD 17.
monuments.certainty: location unknown, near the carceres of the Circus Maximus

monuments.name: Temple of Juno Regina (Aventine)
monuments.summary: Camillus 'called out' Juno, protectress of Veii, by the rite of evocatio before the city fell in 396 BC and dedicated her temple on the Aventine in 392. After lightning struck it in 207 BC the pontiffs had 27 maidens sing a hymn composed by Livius Andronicus. Augustus restored it. Inscriptions found near Santa Sabina locate it approximately.

monuments.name: Temple of Diana (Aventine)
monuments.summary: Attributed to Servius Tullius as a federal sanctuary of the Latin League modelled on the Artemision of Ephesus, outside the pomerium. Its foundation charter, the lex arae Dianae in Aventino, was cited as the model regulation for altars as far afield as Narbo (AD 11) and Salona (137). Gaius Gracchus took refuge here in 121 BC before his death. L. Cornificius rebuilt it after 33 BC.

monuments.name: Temple of Mercury
monuments.summary: Dedicated in 495 BC by the senior centurion M. Laetorius, chosen by the people after the consuls quarrelled over the honour, in the valley of the Circus Maximus by the Aventine slope. It was the seat of the merchants' guild (collegium mercatorum), Mercury being the god of trade; the Mercuralia fell on 15 May, its dedication day.

monuments.name: Temple of Aesculapius (Tiber Island)
monuments.summary: After the plague of 293 BC an embassy to Epidaurus brought back a sacred snake which slipped ashore on the Tiber Island, where the temple was dedicated on 1 January 291 BC. The sick slept in its porticoes; Claudius ruled that slaves abandoned there by their masters became free if they recovered. In the 1st century BC the island's downstream end was faced in travertine as the prow of a ship with a carved snake staff. The church of San Bartolomeo (c. 1000) stands on its site, and a hospital (Fatebenefratelli) still occupies the island.

monuments.name: 'Temple of Minerva Medica'
monuments.summary: A ten-sided domed garden pavilion of the early 4th century, 25 m across, in the Horti Liciniani (probably imperial property of the Licinii, perhaps Gallienus' family), misnamed after a statue thought to be found there. Its brick ribbed dome, partly fallen in 1828, is a key work between the Pantheon and Byzantine architecture.

monuments.name: Circus Maximus
monuments.builderName: traditionally Tarquinius Priscus; rebuilt by Caesar and Trajan

phases.t: Great Fire starts in its shops

monuments.summary: The racetrack in the Murcia valley, laid out by tradition under Tarquinius Priscus; permanent starting gates were built in 329 BC, and the censors of 174 BC added the egg-shaped lap counters. Caesar rebuilt it in 46 BC with a canal (euripus) round the arena, Agrippa added dolphin lap counters (33 BC), and in 10 BC Augustus set on the spina the obelisk of Ramesses II (now Piazza del Popolo). The fire of 64 began in its shops. Trajan's rebuilding made it about 600 by 140 m, the largest entertainment building ever constructed, seating perhaps 150,000 (Pliny's 250,000 may count standing room). Constantius II added a second obelisk of Thutmose III in 357, now at the Lateran. The last recorded races were given by Totila in 549.

monuments.name: Arch of Titus (Circus Maximus)
monuments.summary: A triple arch in the curved end of the Circus Maximus dedicated by the Senate to Titus in 81, shortly before his death. Its inscription, copied in the 8th-century Einsiedeln sylloge, claims Titus 'subdued the Jewish people and destroyed Jerusalem, which all generals, kings and peoples before him had either attacked in vain or not attempted at all', a falsehood given Pompey's capture of 63 BC. Its foundations and column fragments were excavated in 2014-15.

monuments.name: Circus of Maxentius
monuments.summary: Part of Maxentius' villa complex on the Via Appia, with the Mausoleum of his son Romulus, who died in 309. About 520 m long with seats for about 10,000, it is the best-preserved Roman circus, with its towers and starting gates. Its spina carried the obelisk of Domitian that Bernini set on his Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona (1651). It was probably rarely used after Maxentius' fall in 312.

monuments.name: Circus Varianus
monuments.summary: A private circus about 565 m long built by Elagabalus (of the Varii family) beside the Sessorian palace, where the emperor himself drove chariots. The obelisk of Antinous, made under Hadrian, stood on its spina and now stands on the Pincio. The Aurelian Wall cut through it in 271.

monuments.name: Circus of Gaius and Nero (Vatican)

phases.t: obelisk moved to St Peter's Square

monuments.summary: A private circus built by Caligula in the gardens of Agrippina on the Vatican plain, whose spina carried the uninscribed obelisk brought from Alexandria (where it had stood in the Forum Iulium of Cornelius Gallus, as Alföldy showed from its erased inscription); the ship that carried it was later sunk to found the lighthouse at Portus. Nero raced here and in 64 burned Christians as torches in his gardens and circus (Tacitus Ann. 15.44). St Peter's was built just north of it over a cemetery on the adjoining road. The obelisk stood in its place until Domenico Fontana moved it to St Peter's Square in 1586 with 900 men and 140 horses.

monuments.name: Naumachia of Augustus
monuments.summary: An artificial basin of 1,800 by 1,200 Roman feet (about 536 by 357 m) dug in Trastevere for the sea battle of 3,000 men re-enacting Salamis at the dedication of Mars Ultor in 2 BC (Res Gestae 23). Augustus built the non-potable Aqua Alsietina to fill it. Titus staged battles in it in 80. Its exact position near San Cosimato is uncertain.

monuments.name: Amphitheatrum Castrense
monuments.summary: A small brick amphitheatre (88 by 76 m) built in the early 3rd century as part of the imperial Sessorian palace, perhaps for the court's private shows. When the Aurelian Wall was built in 271 it was incorporated into the circuit and its arcades walled up, which is why its outer ring partly survives next to Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

monuments.name: Baths of Titus
monuments.summary: Built hurriedly for the inauguration of the Colosseum in 80 on the Oppian, partly over the Domus Aurea, with a broad stair leading down towards the amphitheatre. Known mainly from Palladio's drawings; Martial praises them.

monuments.name: Baths of Trajan

phases.t: fire in the Domus Aurea wing; site levelled

monuments.summary: Designed by Apollodorus and inaugurated on 22 June 109, two days before the Aqua Traiana, on the Oppian over the Esquiline wing of the Domus Aurea, whose rooms were filled in as foundations after a fire in 104. The 330 by 315 m enclosure with central bath block, palaestrae, libraries and exedrae set the pattern for all later imperial baths; it was oriented to catch the afternoon sun in winter. The Sette Sale cistern held about 8 million litres. The Laocoön group was found in a vineyard nearby in 1506.

monuments.name: Baths of Caracalla (Thermae Antoninianae)
monuments.summary: Begun around 211-212 and dedicated in 216; the outer enclosure was finished by Elagabalus and Severus Alexander. The central block (214 by 110 m) rose over basements with furnaces, storage and a mithraeum, inside an enclosure of about 337 by 328 m with libraries, gardens and stadium seating; some 1,600 bathers could use it at once, fed by a new branch of the Aqua Marcia (Aqua Antoniniana). Its 58 m frigidarium and 35 m domed caldarium were roofed in concrete. The baths worked until the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537. The Farnese Hercules and Farnese Bull were excavated here in 1545-46.

monuments.name: Baths of Decius
monuments.summary: Small baths built by Decius on the Aventine around 250-252, near the earlier private baths of Licinius Sura. Known from Palladio's drawings and a few remains under Piazza del Tempio di Diana.

monuments.name: Baths of Diocletian
monuments.builderName: Maximian in the name of Diocletian

phases.t: water cut in the Gothic siege
Santa Maria degli Angeli by Michelangelo

monuments.summary: The largest baths of Rome, begun by Maximian on his return from Africa in 298 and dedicated in the name of Diocletian and Maximian after their abdication of 1 May 305 by Constantius and Galerius (CIL VI 1130). The enclosure of about 376 by 361 m covered 13 hectares and could serve some 3,000 bathers. Michelangelo transformed the frigidarium into Santa Maria degli Angeli (1561-63); San Bernardo alle Terme occupies a corner rotunda, the Aula Ottagona survives, and the exedra gave its curve to Piazza della Repubblica. It houses part of the Museo Nazionale Romano.

monuments.name: Baths of Constantine

phases.t: earthquake damage; restored by the urban prefect

monuments.summary: The last great imperial baths of Rome, built by Constantine on the Quirinal on a cramped, irregular site. Damaged in the earthquake of 443 and restored by the urban prefect Petronius Perpenna Magnus Quadratianus. Demolished from 1605 for Palazzo Pallavicini-Rospigliosi; its colossal Horse Tamers (Dioscuri) still stand in Piazza del Quirinale, and statues of Constantine and his son from it are on the Capitol.

monuments.name: Baths of Helena (Thermae Helenianae)
monuments.summary: Public baths near the Sessorian palace, restored by Helena, Constantine's mother, after a fire (CIL VI 1136). A large cistern fed by the Aqua Alexandrina survives in Via Eleniana.
monuments.note: Built under the Severans (c. 225); restored by Helena after a fire, c. 325 (CIL VI 1136).

monuments.name: Domus Aurea (Golden House)

phases.t: Otho allots 50 million sesterces to finish it
fire; buried by the Baths of Trajan

monuments.summary: Nero's palace-park built after the fire of 64 by the architects Severus and Celer, with paintings by Famulus, across the Palatine, Velia, Oppian and Caelian, around an artificial lake where the Colosseum now stands; estimates of its extent range from 50 to over 100 hectares. Suetonius describes a vestibule with the Colossus, a mile-long portico, and a revolving dining room; Nero said he could at last live like a human being. The Oppian pavilion, with about 150 rooms including the domed Octagonal Room, survives because Trajan buried it as the foundation of his baths after a fire in 104. Renaissance artists lowered into its 'grottoes' copied its paintings, giving 'grotesques' their name; Raphael's companions left graffiti.

monuments.name: Horti Sallustiani (Gardens of Sallust)
monuments.summary: Gardens in the valley between the Pincian and the Quirinal created by the historian Sallust with money from his governorship of Africa, imperial property from Tiberius on. Nerva died here in 98; Aurelian preferred them to the Palatine. When Alaric's Goths entered by the nearby Porta Salaria on 24 August 410, they burned the house of Sallust (Procopius). The Ludovisi Throne and the Ludovisi Gaul were found here; a domed pavilion survives in Piazza Sallustio.

monuments.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian (Castel Sant'Angelo)

phases.t: burial of Caracalla, the last emperor interred

monuments.summary: Begun by Hadrian around 130 across the Tiber in the Ager Vaticanus and completed by Antoninus Pius in 139, who moved Hadrian's ashes from Puteoli: a square base about 89 m wide supporting a drum 64 m across and 21 m high, topped by a garden mound and a quadriga. Antoninus, Faustina, Lucius Aelius, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus, Commodus, Septimius Severus and lastly Caracalla (217) were buried here. Incorporated into the Aurelian Wall as a bridgehead fort, it was defended against the Goths in 537 by troops who hurled its statues down on the attackers (Procopius 5.22). The later legend of Gregory the Great's vision of the Archangel Michael sheathing his sword over it during the plague of 590 gave it its name. It became the papal fortress.

monuments.name: Tomb of the Scipios
monuments.summary: The rock-cut family tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones on the Via Appia, begun in the early 3rd century BC, probably by L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus (consul 298), whose peperino sarcophagus with its Saturnian verse elogium is now in the Vatican. Burials continued to about 150 BC, with a later façade and Imperial reuse. Livy says a statue of Ennius stood here. It was found in 1614 and excavated in 1780.

monuments.name: Pyramid of Cestius
monuments.summary: The tomb of C. Cestius Epulo, praetor, tribune and member of the septemviri epulones, a 36.4 m pyramid in brick-faced concrete clad in Luna marble, built, its inscription says, in 330 days in accordance with his will. Agrippa is named among his heirs, so it predates 12 BC. Egyptomania after the conquest of Egypt shaped its form, though it is steeper than Giza's pyramids, like the Nubian ones. Built into the Aurelian Wall in 271, it survives beside the Porta Ostiensis and the Protestant Cemetery.

monuments.name: Tomb of Caecilia Metella
monuments.summary: A drum tomb 29.5 m in diameter on the third mile of the Via Appia, built around 30-10 BC for Caecilia Metella, daughter of Q. Caecilius Metellus Creticus and wife of M. Licinius Crassus, son of the triumvir. Its frieze of ox skulls gave the area the name Capo di Bove. The Caetani turned it into the keep of a fortress astride the road in 1302.

monuments.name: Tomb of Eurysaces the Baker
monuments.summary: The tomb of M. Vergilius Eurysaces, a freedman baker and public contractor, built around 50-20 BC at the fork of the Via Praenestina and Labicana, its cylinders resembling dough-mixing vessels and its frieze showing every stage of bread-making. It was swallowed by an Honorian tower of the Porta Maggiore and revealed when Gregory XVI demolished the tower in 1838.

monuments.name: Mausoleum of Constantina (Santa Costanza)

phases.t: burial of Helena, wife of Julian

monuments.summary: A domed rotunda with ambulatory built around 340-350 beside the basilica of Sant'Agnese on the Via Nomentana for Constantine's daughter Constantina (died 354), and later her sister Helena, wife of Julian. Its barrel-vault mosaics of vintaging putti and birds are among the finest of the 4th century; her porphyry sarcophagus is in the Vatican. It became the church of Santa Costanza in 1254.

monuments.name: Mausoleum of Helena (Tor Pignattara)
monuments.summary: A domed rotunda about 20 m in diameter on the Via Labicana, built about 326-330 against the basilica of Saints Marcellinus and Peter on the imperial estate ad duas lauros, probably first intended for Constantine himself. Helena was buried here in a porphyry sarcophagus carved with Roman cavalry riding down barbarians (a military theme suited to an emperor), now in the Vatican. The name Tor Pignattara comes from the amphorae (pignatte) set in the vault to lighten it.

monuments.name: Aqua Appia
monuments.summary: Rome's first aqueduct, built by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus in 312 BC with the Via Appia: about 16.4 km long, almost entirely underground, from springs near the 7th-8th mile of the Via Praenestina, entering the city at Spes Vetus and ending at the Porta Trigemina by the Forum Boarium and the salt depots. It delivered about 73,000 cubic metres a day by Frontinus' figures.
monuments.certainty: terminus at the Porta Trigemina approximate

monuments.name: Anio Vetus
monuments.summary: The second aqueduct, taking water from the Anio river above Tibur, about 64 km long and almost entirely underground. Contracted in 272 BC by the censor M'. Curius Dentatus from the spoils of Pyrrhus, it was finished in 269 by M. Fulvius Flaccus after Curius died. Its muddy water went to gardens and fountains rather than drinking. It entered Rome near Spes Vetus and distributed on the Esquiline.

monuments.name: Aqua Marcia

phases.t: branch to the Baths of Diocletian

monuments.summary: Built in 144-140 BC by the praetor Q. Marcius Rex, voted 180 million sesterces, after the Decemviri warned from the Sibylline Books against bringing water to the Capitol. At 91 km from springs in the upper Anio valley it was the longest of the Republic, with 10 km on arches, the first high-level aqueduct, and its water was prized as the coldest and purest (Pliny). Its arches carry the Tepula and Julia over the Augustan arch later built into the Porta Tiburtina, inscribed with restorations by Augustus (5 BC), Titus (79) and Caracalla (212), who added the Aqua Antoniniana branch to his baths.
monuments.certainty: placed at its city entry at the Porta Tiburtina arch

monuments.name: Aqua Virgo

phases.t: Arch of Claudius rebuilds its arcade

monuments.summary: Opened by Agrippa on 9 June 19 BC to feed his baths: 21 km almost all underground, entering the city from the north on arches (the Arch of Claudius on the Via Lata was one) and ending in the Campus Martius by the Saepta. Frontinus says a girl showed the soldiers the spring, hence the name. Cut by the Goths in 537, it was the first restored in the Middle Ages and is the only ancient aqueduct to have run almost continuously; its modern outlet is the Trevi Fountain (1732-62), shown here.

monuments.name: Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus
monuments.builderName: begun by Caligula; completed by Claudius

phases.t: out of service until Vespasian's repairs

monuments.summary: Two aqueducts begun by Caligula in 38 and dedicated by Claudius on 1 August 52: the Claudia, 69 km from springs near Subiaco, and the Anio Novus, 87 km from the river, the largest of all. For their last 15 km they ran on a single arcade up to 27 m high, the Anio Novus in a channel above the Claudia, the arcade that dominates the Campagna. They met the city at Spes Vetus over the double arch later called Porta Maggiore, whose attic carries Claudius' inscription and the restorations of Vespasian (71, after nine years out of use) and Titus (81). Nero's Arcus Caelimontani carried a branch to the Caelian and Palatine.

monuments.name: Aqua Traiana
monuments.summary: Inaugurated by Trajan on 24 June 109, bringing spring water 57 km from the hills around Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum, where it drove the grain mills that ground the city's bread. When Witigis cut the aqueducts in 537, Belisarius mounted mills on boats moored in the Tiber current (Procopius 5.19). Paul V restored it as the Acqua Paola (1612), whose great fountain on the Janiculum marks the terminus.

monuments.name: Nymphaeum of Alexander ('Trofei di Mario')
monuments.summary: A monumental fountain and distribution castellum of the Aqua Julia branch built by Severus Alexander, dated by coins of 226, at the junction of two roads on the Esquiline in today's Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II. Its two marble trophies, wrongly attributed to Marius, were moved to the Capitol balustrade in 1590.

monuments.name: 'Arch of Drusus'
monuments.summary: An aqueduct arch carrying the Aqua Antoniniana over the Via Appia just inside the later Porta Appia, built by Caracalla around 212. Antiquarians identified it with the arch voted to Drusus the Elder on the Appia in 9 BC, a name that stuck.

monuments.name: Pons Sublicius
monuments.summary: Rome's oldest bridge, attributed to Ancus Marcius: wooden and held together without metal for ritual reasons, maintained by the pontifices, whose name may mean 'bridge-makers'. Horatius Cocles held it against Porsenna in 508 BC while it was cut down behind him. Each May the Vestals threw the straw Argei figures into the river from it. Floods swept it away in 23 BC and AD 69, but it was always rebuilt in wood and is listed in the 4th-century Regionaries. Its site below the Pons Aemilius by the Forum Boarium is debated.

monuments.name: Pons Aemilius (Ponte Rotto)
monuments.summary: The first stone bridge in Rome: the censors of 179 BC, M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior, built the stone piers, and the censors of 142 BC, Scipio Aemilianus and L. Mummius, added the arches. Rebuilt under Augustus, it carried traffic from the Forum Boarium to Trastevere. After floods in 1557 and 1598 carried away its eastern arches, a single arch has stood midstream ever since, the 'broken bridge'.

monuments.name: Pons Fabricius

phases.t: repairs by the consuls of 21 BC

monuments.summary: Built in 62 BC by L. Fabricius, curator viarum, to replace a wooden bridge to the Tiber Island; his name is inscribed on both faces, along with a repair by the consuls M. Lollius and Q. Lepidus in 21 BC. With two arches spanning 24.5 m and a flood arch in the central pier, it is the oldest Roman bridge in Rome still in use in its original form. The four-headed herms on the parapet give it the name Ponte dei Quattro Capi.

monuments.name: Pons Cestius (Pons Gratiani)
monuments.summary: The bridge from the Tiber Island to Trastevere, built in the 1st century BC, probably by a L. Cestius. Valentinian, Valens and Gratian rebuilt it in 365-370, and the inscription names it Pons Gratiani. It was dismantled and rebuilt in 1888-92 for the Tiber embankments, keeping the central arch's form with much original stone.

monuments.name: Pons Milvius

phases.t: crowds await news of the Metaurus at the wooden bridge

monuments.summary: The bridge carrying the Via Flaminia across the Tiber north of the city, rebuilt in stone in 109 BC by the censor M. Aemilius Scaurus to replace a wooden bridge where crowds had waited for news of the Metaurus in 207 BC. Here on the night of 2-3 December 63 BC Cicero's praetors arrested the Allobrogan envoys with letters from the Catilinarians. On 28 October 312 Maxentius, fighting before it with a pontoon bridge behind him, was routed by Constantine and drowned. The central arches are ancient.

monuments.name: Pons Aelius (Ponte Sant'Angelo)
monuments.summary: Built by Hadrian in 134 as the monumental approach to his mausoleum, with ramps on either bank; the three central arches are original. Medieval pilgrims to St Peter's crowded it; during the Jubilee of 1450 a parapet collapsed under a panicked crowd and some 170 people died. Clement IX had Bernini's workshop add the ten angels with the instruments of the Passion in 1669.

monuments.name: Pons Neronianus
monuments.summary: A bridge linking the Campus Martius to the Vatican gardens and Nero's circus, built under Caligula or Nero. It was already in ruins by late antiquity; its pier foundations are visible at low water just downstream of Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II.

monuments.name: Pons Aurelius (Pons Agrippae / Ponte Sisto)
monuments.summary: A bridge first built by Agrippa (a curatorial cippus naming a pons Agrippae was found here in 1887), later called Pons Aurelius, and rebuilt in 365-367 by Valentinian I as the Pons Valentiniani, adorned with statues. It collapsed in 792; Sixtus IV rebuilt it in 1473-79 as Ponte Sisto.

monuments.name: Pons Probi (Pons Theodosii)
monuments.summary: The southernmost bridge, near the Aventine and Emporium, probably built by Probus and rebuilt by Theodosius I in the 380s. It collapsed in the Middle Ages and its remains were cleared in 1877-78.
monuments.certainty: location approximate; date of collapse unknown
